Zobellviridae.note: A tailed bacteriophage (class Caudoviricetes): icosahedral head of packaged DNA, a tail that docks on the cell wall, and fibres that select the host.

Inoviridae.note: Long thin filaments extruded from the host without killing it; M13 is the backbone of phage display.

Anelloviridae.note: Circular negative-sense ssDNA, carried by most healthy humans for life with no established disease — the bulk of the human 'virome'.

Polyomaviridae.note: Circular dsDNA; large T antigen drives the cell cycle, which makes these viruses both oncogenic and classic tools of cell biology.

Papillomaviridae.note: A small circular dsDNA genome in a T=7 capsid of L1 pentamers. In high-risk types E6 and E7 inactivate p53 and Rb — the basis of cervical cancer, and L1 is the vaccine antigen.

Parvoviridae.note: Among the smallest animal viruses. The single-stranded DNA genome needs cells in S phase to replicate, which is why B19 targets erythroid precursors.

Circoviridae.note: A tiny circular ssDNA genome replicated by rolling-circle synthesis.

Smacoviridae.note: Small circular ssDNA viruses found in faecal samples.

Nanoviridae.note: Each of the eight circular ssDNA components is packaged in its own particle, so a complete infection requires all of them to arrive in the same cell.

Geminiviridae.note: Twinned incomplete icosahedra — two joined particles, the geminate morphology that names the family.

Genomoviridae.note: Circular ssDNA viruses of fungi and other hosts.

Sedoreoviridae.note: A smooth triple-layered particle. Rotavirus's 11 segments reassort freely, which is why strains are typed by two independent genes (G and P).

Spinareoviridae.note: Turreted capsid: spikes at the icosahedral vertices cap the channels through which mRNA is extruded.

Hepeviridae.note: Naked in faeces but quasi-enveloped in blood, cloaked in host membrane — which changes how antibodies can reach it.

Matonaviridae.note: Rubella virus alone: an alphavirus-like architecture but a respiratory, non-arthropod-borne lifestyle and a notorious teratogen.

Bromoviridae.note: Tripartite plant RNA viruses; all three segments must enter a cell for infection.

Closteroviridae.note: Very long flexuous filaments with the largest plant RNA genomes, confined to the phloem.

Togaviridae.note: A strikingly regular particle: 80 trimeric E1/E2 spikes in T=4 symmetry over an icosahedral capsid. Non-structural genes are translated first, structural genes from a subgenomic RNA.

Virgaviridae.note: Rigid helical rods. Tobacco mosaic virus, in this family, was the first virus ever described and the first to be crystallised.

Flaviviridae.note: A smooth envelope with E glycoprotein lying flat in a herringbone lattice rather than projecting spikes. One long polyprotein is cleaved into three structural and seven non-structural proteins.

Hepaciviridae.note: Unusually ill-defined for a virus this well studied: hepatitis C circulates bound to host lipoproteins as a lipoviroparticle, so its density varies, its diameter is reported across a wide range, and no high-resolution structure of the whole virion exists. E1/E2 heterodimers form the spikes, and the single polyprotein is cleaved into three structural and seven non-structural proteins -- NS3/4A and NS5A and NS5B being the targets of the drugs that cure it.

Narnaviridae.note: Capsidless RNA replicons of fungi — a naked ribonucleoprotein with no virion stage.

Mitoviridae.note: Capsidless: the genome replicates inside fungal mitochondria as naked RNA and spreads only by cell fusion, never forming a particle at all.

Atkinsviridae.note: A small naked icosahedral positive-sense RNA phage of the Leviviricetes — a genome of only three or four genes, among the simplest replicating entities known.

Duinviridae.note: A small naked icosahedral positive-sense RNA phage of the Leviviricetes — a genome of only three or four genes, among the simplest replicating entities known.

Fiersviridae.note: Tiny positive-sense RNA phages; MS2 and Qβ, whose coat protein and replicase underpinned early molecular genetics.

Solspiviridae.note: A small naked icosahedral positive-sense RNA phage of the Leviviricetes — a genome of only three or four genes, among the simplest replicating entities known.

Steitzviridae.note: Single-stranded RNA phages related to the Qβ group, now the largest described family by species count.

Botourmiaviridae.note: Mostly mycoviruses, plus some plant viruses.

Bornaviridae.note: Unusually for a negative-sense RNA virus, replicates and splices its transcripts in the nucleus.

Filoviridae.note: Long filaments, often hooked or 6-shaped, up to a micrometre — among the largest animal virus particles, visible by light microscopy.

Paramyxoviridae.note: Pleomorphic envelope with two surface glycoproteins: one binds the receptor, the other (F) fuses membranes, which is why these viruses form syncytia.

Pneumoviridae.note: Filamentous and spherical forms with G attachment and F fusion proteins; F is the target of RSV monoclonals and vaccines.

Rhabdoviridae.note: A rigid bullet-shaped particle: helical nucleocapsid wound inside a bullet envelope studded with a single trimeric G glycoprotein, the target of rabies vaccines.

Fimoviridae.note: Emaraviruses carry four to eight segments; the number varies between species, so the figure follows the ICTV accession list where one is given.

Hantaviridae.note: Tri-segmented like other bunyavirals, but with a grid-like surface lattice of Gn/Gc spikes and no arthropod vector — transmission is by rodent excreta.

Peribunyaviridae.note: Three negative-sense segments (L, M, S) in a lipid envelope. Because the genome is in three pieces, co-infecting strains can swap whole segments — the reassortment that produced Ngari and Iquitos viruses.

Arenaviridae.note: Two ambisense segments, and ribosomes scavenged from the host cell are visible inside the particle — the sandy granules that name the family.

Nairoviridae.note: The largest bunyaviral L segment, encoding an ovarian-tumour protease domain that strips ubiquitin from host immune signalling proteins.

Phenuiviridae.note: The S segment is ambisense: N and the interferon-antagonist NSs are read in opposite directions from the same RNA.

Amnoonviridae.note: Tilapia lake virus: ten segments with almost no sequence similarity to other orthomyxo-like viruses.

Orthomyxoviridae.note: Eight separate segments, each a ribonucleoprotein. Two co-infecting strains can exchange segments wholesale — antigenic shift, the mechanism behind influenza pandemics.

Picobirnaviridae.note: Bisegmented dsRNA viruses found in faeces; whether the host is the animal or its gut bacteria is unresolved.

Hadakaviridae.note: Hadaka virus is capsidless — “hadaka” means naked — with eleven segments and no virion to draw.

Coronaviridae.note: The club-shaped spike trimers that form the 'corona'. At ~30 kb these are among the largest RNA genomes, which requires a proofreading exonuclease to replicate at all.

Caliciviridae.note: Cup-shaped surface depressions give the family its name; the naked capsid survives chlorination and makes norovirus extraordinarily transmissible.

Picornaviridae.note: A small, rugged, naked icosahedron of 60 copies each of four capsid proteins — stable in stomach acid, which is how enteroviruses reach the gut.

Secoviridae.note: Nematode- and beetle-transmitted plant viruses with a bipartite genome.

Potyviridae.note: Flexuous filaments spread by aphids; the largest family of plant RNA viruses.

Astroviridae.note: A five- or six-pointed star outline on electron microscopy.

Hepadnaviridae.note: A partially double-stranded circular DNA genome replicated via RNA. Infected cells shed vast excesses of empty surface-antigen particles — the HBsAg measured in serology.

Caulimoviridae.note: Plant viruses that reverse transcribe like retroviruses but package DNA; many are endogenised in plant genomes.

Retroviridae.note: Two copies of the RNA genome, reverse transcriptase and integrase inside a conical core. Integration into host DNA makes infection permanent.

Kolmioviridae.note: Hepatitis delta: a circular RNA encoding one protein, which borrows hepatitis B surface antigen as its envelope and so cannot spread without it.

Phycodnaviridae.note: Large dsDNA viruses of eukaryotic algae.

Mimiviridae.note: Giant viruses of amoebae, large enough to see by light microscopy and bearing a dense fibre fringe. Their genomes encode translation components once thought exclusive to cells.

Iridoviridae.note: Large icosahedral viruses of invertebrates and fish; purified pellets diffract light, hence 'irido'.

Poxviridae.note: A brick-shaped particle with a dumbbell core and lateral bodies. Uniquely for a DNA virus it replicates entirely in the cytoplasm, carrying its own transcription machinery.

Adenoviridae.note: A naked icosahedron with an antenna-like fibre at each of the twelve vertices — the receptor-binding structure exploited by adenoviral vector vaccines.

Baculoviridae.note: Rod-shaped insect viruses occluded in protein crystals; the basis of the baculovirus protein expression system.

Alphasatellitidae.note: Satellite DNA components reliant on a helper virus.

Ampullaviridae.note: Bottle-shaped archaeal virus from an acidic hot spring.

Bicaudaviridae.note: A lemon-shaped particle that grows a tail at each end after leaving the cell — development outside a host, which is unique among viruses.

Clavaviridae.note: A rigid rod with a cap at one end only.

Fuselloviridae.note: Lemon-shaped archaeal virus with short tail fibres at one pole, from acidic hot springs.

Plasmaviridae.note: One of the few enveloped bacteriophages.

Polydnaviriformidae.note: Encoded in the genome of parasitoid wasps and injected with their eggs to suppress host caterpillar immunity — a virus domesticated as a weapon.

I.label: dsDNA
I.name: Group I — double-stranded DNA
I.strategy: Transcribed directly by host (or virus-encoded) RNA polymerase. Most replicate in the nucleus and many encode their own DNA polymerase.
I.examples: Herpesviruses, poxviruses, adenoviruses, papillomaviruses, most bacteriophages

II.label: ssDNA
II.name: Group II — single-stranded DNA
II.strategy: The strand is converted to a double-stranded intermediate before transcription, usually by host machinery, which restricts replication to dividing cells for several families.

V.label: ssRNA(-)
V.name: Group V — negative-sense single-stranded RNA
V.strategy: Cannot be translated. The virion must deliver its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and the genome stays coated in nucleoprotein throughout. Segmented members can reassort.
V.examples: Influenza viruses, paramyxoviruses, rhabdoviruses, filoviruses, bunyaviruses, arenaviruses

III.label: dsRNA
III.name: Group III — double-stranded RNA
III.strategy: Transcribed inside an intact capsid by a virion-packaged polymerase: the dsRNA is never exposed to the cytoplasm, where it would trigger innate sensors.

IV.label: ssRNA(+)
IV.name: Group IV — positive-sense single-stranded RNA
IV.strategy: The genome IS mRNA: naked RNA entering a cell is infectious. Translated immediately, then copied through a negative-sense intermediate on membranous replication organelles.

VII.label: dsDNA-RT
VII.name: Group VII — dsDNA with reverse transcriptase
VII.strategy: A DNA genome replicated through an RNA intermediate by reverse transcriptase. The covalently closed circular DNA form persists in the nucleus and is why hepatitis B is so hard to cure.
VII.examples: Hepatitis B virus, other hepadnaviruses, caulimoviruses

VI.label: ssRNA-RT
VI.name: Group VI — positive-sense ssRNA with reverse transcriptase
VI.strategy: Reverse-transcribed to DNA and integrated into the host genome as a provirus, which is why infection is lifelong and why integration site matters.
VI.examples: HIV-1 and HIV-2, HTLV-1, other retroviruses

Simplexvirus humanalpha1.tropism: Mucosal epithelium, then sensory neurons of the trigeminal ganglion where latency is established.
Simplexvirus humanalpha1.entry: gD binding plus the gB/gH-gL core fusion machinery; plasma-membrane fusion in neurons, endocytic in some epithelia.
Simplexvirus humanalpha1.note: Nectin-1 at neuronal junctions is what gives HSV access to axon terminals, hence lifelong ganglionic latency and recurrence at the same dermatome.

Varicellovirus humanalpha3.tropism: T cells (which carry it to skin), keratinocytes, dorsal root ganglia.
Varicellovirus humanalpha3.note: T-cell-mediated spread to skin explains the diffuse exanthem of chickenpox, and dorsal-root latency the dermatomal distribution of zoster decades later.

receptors: Neuropilin-2 with CD147 (epithelium, endothelium, via the pentamer)
Cytomegalovirus humanbeta5.tropism: Fibroblasts, endothelium, epithelium, monocytes, placental trophoblast.
Cytomegalovirus humanbeta5.entry: Trimer gH/gL/gO for fibroblasts; pentamer gH/gL/UL128-130-131 for epithelial, endothelial and myeloid cells.
Cytomegalovirus humanbeta5.note: The trimer/pentamer distinction is why laboratory strains passaged on fibroblasts lose the pentamer and epithelial tropism, and why pentamer-containing immunogens are central to congenital CMV vaccine efforts.

receptors: CD21 (CR2) with HLA class II for B cells
Ephrin receptor A2 for epithelial cells
Lymphocryptovirus humangamma4.entry: gp350/CD21 attachment, then gH/gL/gp42-mediated fusion; gp42 is required for B cells and inhibitory for epithelium.
Lymphocryptovirus humangamma4.note: The gp42 switch means virus made in B cells preferentially infects epithelium and vice versa — an elegant mechanism for shuttling between the two compartments, and the basis of lifelong carriage.

receptors: LSTc glycan (α2,6-sialylated lactoseries tetrasaccharide c) — attachment, required by all genotypes
Betapolyomavirus secuhominis.tropism: Renal tubular epithelium; oligodendrocytes and astrocytes in the brain.
Betapolyomavirus secuhominis.entry: LSTc engagement, then 5-HT2A-dependent clathrin-mediated endocytosis; soluble LSTc blocks infection.
Betapolyomavirus secuhominis.note: The two act in sequence rather than as alternatives, which is how they were written here. JC virus binds b-series gangliosides weakly, but they are not required for infection; GT1b and GD1b belong to BK virus, which is a different species. Oligodendrocyte tropism gives progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy; the dependence on immunosuppression explains why PML follows natalizumab, rituximab and advanced HIV.

receptors: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans, then a secondary receptor after furin cleavage of L2
Alphapapillomavirus 9.tropism: Basal keratinocytes of squamous and transformation-zone epithelium, reached through a microwound.
Alphapapillomavirus 9.entry: Slow, multi-hour: HSPG binding, conformational change, L2 cleavage, endocytosis, and nuclear delivery that requires mitosis.
Alphapapillomavirus 9.note: Entry needs access to the basal layer and a dividing cell, which is why HPV targets the cervical transformation zone and why the prophylactic vaccines, acting on L1 before basement-membrane engagement, are so effective.

receptors: Histo-blood group antigens (VP8* of genotype-dependent specificity)
Rotavirus alphagastroenteritidis.tropism: Mature enterocytes at the villus tip of the small intestine.
Rotavirus alphagastroenteritidis.entry: Sequential VP8*/VP5* interactions; trypsin cleavage of VP4 is required, which is why the gut is the permissive site.
Rotavirus alphagastroenteritidis.note: P[8] human strains bind secretor-dependent HBGAs, so FUT2 status shapes both susceptibility and oral vaccine take — part of why rotavirus vaccine efficacy differs between high- and low-income settings.

attachment: MOG (myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein) — proposed, and cannot account for the tropism
Rubivirus rubellae.tropism: Respiratory epithelium, then placenta and fetal tissues.
Rubivirus rubellae.note: MOG was reported as a receptor in 2011 on the strength of E1 binding and of conferring permissiveness on 293T cells, and it is still the only candidate named — but MOG is expressed essentially only in oligodendrocytes, keratinocytes without surface MOG are infected, and it therefore cannot explain respiratory or placental entry. Listing it as the receptor contradicted the tropism printed beside it. Placental and fetal tropism in the first trimester produces congenital rubella syndrome; maternal infection after 20 weeks rarely does.

Alphavirus chikungunya.tropism: Fibroblasts, synovial tissue, muscle, skin; not neurotropic in adults.
Alphavirus chikungunya.note: MXRA8 is expressed on joint fibroblasts, synovium and osteoblasts — a direct explanation for the months-to-years polyarthralgia that makes chikungunya distinctive among arboviral fevers.

Orthoflavivirus flavi.tropism: Dendritic cells, then hepatocytes, myocardium and kidney.
Orthoflavivirus flavi.note: Hepatocyte tropism gives the jaundice and coagulopathy that make yellow fever viscerotropic rather than simply febrile.

Orthoflavivirus denguei.tropism: Dermal dendritic cells first, then monocytes, macrophages and liver; endothelium is affected largely without infection.
Orthoflavivirus denguei.note: No single high-affinity receptor is established, which matters: entry via Fcγ receptors on monocytes during antibody-dependent enhancement is the mechanism behind severe secondary dengue, and is what the licensed vaccines have to be positioned around. Dengvaxia is given only to people with confirmed prior dengue infection. Qdenga needs no pre-vaccination screening — its EU indication is simply everyone from 4 years of age — but WHO restricts programmatic use to high-transmission settings, because efficacy against DENV-3 and DENV-4 in the seronegative is less certain.

Orthoflavivirus zikaense.tropism: Dermal fibroblasts and keratinocytes, neural progenitor cells, placental cytotrophoblasts and Hofbauer cells, testis, retina.
Orthoflavivirus zikaense.note: AXL is highly expressed on radial glial neural progenitors and on placental cells, which is the clearest mechanistic link to microcephaly and congenital Zika syndrome — though AXL knockouts remain infectible, so it is facilitating rather than strictly required.

Orthoebolavirus zairense.tropism: Monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, then hepatocytes, adrenal cortex and endothelium.
Orthoebolavirus zairense.entry: Macropinocytosis, then cathepsin B/L cleavage of GP exposes the receptor-binding site for NPC1 in late endosomes.
Orthoebolavirus zairense.note: The receptor is intracellular, so nothing binds Ebola at the cell surface in a blockable way — one reason entry inhibitors have been hard, and why the successful therapeutics are monoclonals against GP (ansuvimab, the REGN-EB3 cocktail).

Orthomarburgvirus marburgense.note: Same NPC1 dependence as Ebola, with no licensed countermeasure.

Henipavirus hendraense.note: Same receptors as Nipah, hence the same vasculitis-and-encephalitis picture acquired from horses.

Henipavirus nipahense.tropism: Endothelium of small vessels, neurons, and respiratory epithelium.
Henipavirus nipahense.entry: Direct fusion at the plasma membrane via G and F.
Henipavirus nipahense.note: Ephrin-B2/B3 are extraordinarily conserved across mammals, which is why Nipah crosses species barriers so easily and why its host range is so wide. Ephrin-B3 expression in brainstem neurons matches the encephalitis, and endothelial ephrin-B2 the vasculitis.

Morbillivirus hominis.tropism: Activated T and B cells, dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages first (SLAM); then basolateral airway epithelium (nectin-4) for shedding into the lumen.
Morbillivirus hominis.entry: Direct fusion at the plasma membrane, pH-independent, via the H and F glycoproteins.
Morbillivirus hominis.note: The two-receptor sequence explains measles precisely: SLAM entry into immune memory cells causes the profound lymphopenia and 'immune amnesia' that drives post-measles mortality, while nectin-4 on the basolateral epithelial surface explains why a systemic infection ends up as the most transmissible respiratory virus known. CD46 use by vaccine strains is an artefact of Vero adaptation, not wild-type biology.

attachment: Heparan sulfate (cultured cells; minor in vivo)
Orthopneumovirus hominis.tropism: Ciliated apical airway epithelium; syncytium formation.
Orthopneumovirus hominis.entry: Fusion at the plasma membrane or via macropinocytosis, driven by F.
Orthopneumovirus hominis.note: CX3CR1 on ciliated cells is the physiological receptor; heparan sulfate dominates in immortalised cell lines and misled early tropism work. The prefusion F conformation is the target of both nirsevimab and the licensed older-adult vaccines.

Lyssavirus rabies.tropism: Skeletal muscle at the inoculation site, then peripheral nerve and CNS neurons.
Lyssavirus rabies.entry: Endocytosis and low-pH G-mediated fusion; retrograde axonal transport to the CNS.
Lyssavirus rabies.note: Binding the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction is how rabies gets into a motor neuron, and retrograde transport is why incubation depends on distance from the brain — and why wound washing plus immunoglobulin at the bite site still works days later.

Orthohantavirus sinnombreense.note: PCDH1 dependence on lung endothelium is a strong explanation for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: the capillary leak is driven by endothelial dysfunction, largely without cytopathology.

Mammarenavirus lassaense.entry: α-dystroglycan binding, endocytosis, then a pH-dependent switch to LAMP1 in the late endosome.
Mammarenavirus lassaense.note: The two-receptor hand-off is unusual and explains why Old World arenaviruses need an acidified compartment; New World haemorrhagic fever arenaviruses instead use transferrin receptor 1, and human TfR1 compatibility is what makes Junín, Machupo, Guanarito, Sabiá and Chapare human pathogens while their relatives are not.

Mammarenavirus juninense.note: Use of human TfR1 is the molecular basis of pathogenicity for the South American haemorrhagic fever arenaviruses — a single receptor preference separating lethal viruses from harmless relatives.

receptors: Sialic acid, α2,3-linked (avian enteric and human lower airway)
Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae.tropism: Human: α2,6 on upper airway epithelium. Avian viruses prefer α2,3, found on human type II pneumocytes, alveolar macrophages and conjunctiva.
Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae.entry: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis, then low-pH-triggered HA2 fusion; M2 acidifies the virion to release the ribonucleoprotein.
Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae.note: This single preference governs pandemic risk. H5N1 binds α2,3 in the human deep lung and conjunctiva, which explains severe pneumonia, conjunctivitis in dairy-outbreak cases, and poor human-to-human transmission: there is little α2,3 in the upper airway for exhaled droplets to come from. A switch to α2,6 is the change surveillance watches for.

Betainfluenzavirus influenzae.note: No animal reservoir of consequence, so no reassortment-driven antigenic shift — influenza B drifts but does not cause pandemics.

Alphacoronavirus chicagoense.note: A common-cold coronavirus; APN use and upper-airway restriction keep it mild in the immunocompetent.

Alphacoronavirus amsterdamense.tropism: Upper airway, with croup in young children.
Alphacoronavirus amsterdamense.note: Uses the same receptor as SARS-CoV-2 but a quite different spike, and causes trivial disease — a useful corrective to the idea that the receptor alone determines severity.

Betacoronavirus cameli.tropism: Lower respiratory epithelium and type II pneumocytes; little upper-airway expression in humans.
Betacoronavirus cameli.entry: TMPRSS2 or cathepsin-dependent fusion after spike cleavage.
Betacoronavirus cameli.note: DPP4 in humans is abundant in the deep lung but sparse in the upper airway, which is exactly why MERS is severe when it takes and yet transmits badly outside hospitals.

Betacoronavirus pandemicum.tropism: Nasal ciliated epithelium, type II pneumocytes, enterocytes, vascular endothelium, renal tubules.
Betacoronavirus pandemicum.entry: Two routes: TMPRSS2-mediated cleavage and fusion at the plasma membrane, or cathepsin-L-dependent endosomal fusion. The furin site at S1/S2 pre-activates spike.
Betacoronavirus pandemicum.note: ACE2 distribution maps onto the clinical syndrome — anosmia, pneumonia, diarrhoea, thrombosis, renal injury. Which of the two entry routes dominates is cell-type dependent and shifted with Omicron toward the endosomal route, which tracks its more upper-airway, less pneumotropic behaviour.

Norovirus norwalkense.tropism: Small intestinal enterocytes and tuft cells.
Norovirus norwalkense.note: HBGA dependence is why susceptibility is genetically determined: FUT2 non-secretors are resistant to GII.4 norovirus, which is one of the few human infections with a clean Mendelian resistance locus.

Enterovirus alpharhino.tropism: Upper airway epithelium; replicates best at 33–35 °C.
Enterovirus alpharhino.entry: Endocytosis; ICAM-1 binding destabilises the capsid.
Enterovirus alpharhino.note: Temperature optimum plus ICAM-1 distribution confine rhinovirus A/B to the nose and throat. Rhinovirus C uses CDHR3 instead, is not temperature-restricted in the same way, and reaches the lower airway — which is why it dominates asthma exacerbations in children.

Enterovirus betacoxsackie.note: CAR on cardiomyocytes is the basis of enteroviral myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy.

Enterovirus cerhino.tropism: Ciliated lower as well as upper airway epithelium.
Enterovirus cerhino.note: The CDHR3 rs6967330 asthma-risk allele increases surface expression and rhinovirus C binding — one of the cleanest host-genetics-to-virus links in respiratory medicine.

Enterovirus coxsackiepol.tropism: Intestinal epithelium and lymphoid tissue, then anterior horn motor neurons.
Enterovirus coxsackiepol.entry: CD155 binding triggers uncoating at the membrane or in early endosomes.
Enterovirus coxsackiepol.note: CD155 expression on motor neurons explains the paralysis, and its absence in most mammals is why transgenic CD155 mice had to be made to model poliomyelitis.

Hepatovirus ahepa.entry: Endolysosomal; gangliosides act in the lysosome rather than at the plasma membrane.
Hepatovirus ahepa.note: HAV circulates both naked and cloaked in host membrane (quasi-enveloped), which lets it evade neutralising antibody while remaining acid-stable enough for faecal-oral spread.

Orthohepadnavirus hominoidei.entry: preS1 domain of large surface protein binds NTCP; endocytosis and nuclear delivery of relaxed circular DNA, converted to cccDNA.
Orthohepadnavirus hominoidei.note: NTCP is a bile-acid transporter expressed almost only on hepatocytes, which accounts for HBV's strict hepatotropism and narrow host range. It is directly druggable: bulevirtide is an NTCP-blocking preS1 lipopeptide licensed for hepatitis D.

Deltaretrovirus priTlym1.tropism: CD4+ T cells, infected by cell-to-cell contact.
Deltaretrovirus priTlym1.entry: Fusion at cell-cell contacts; free virions are poorly infectious.
Deltaretrovirus priTlym1.note: HTLV-1 spreads almost entirely cell-to-cell through a virological synapse and biofilm, so plasma viral load is low and transmission requires cellular material — breastfeeding, transfusion of cellular products, sexual contact.

Lentivirus humimdef1.tropism: CD4+ T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, microglia.
Lentivirus humimdef1.entry: Direct fusion at the plasma membrane after CD4 binding exposes the coreceptor-binding site and releases gp41.
Lentivirus humimdef1.note: The coreceptor switch is clinically central: CCR5-tropic viruses dominate transmission, which is why CCR5-Δ32 homozygotes resist infection, why maraviroc works only against R5 virus, and why the Berlin and London cures used CCR5-Δ32 donor marrow. X4 emergence marks accelerated CD4 decline.

receptors: NTCP / SLC10A1, via the HBV envelope
Deltavirus italiense.entry: Borrowed HBsAg envelope; entry identical to HBV.
Deltavirus italiense.note: HDV has no envelope of its own, so it is wholly dependent on HBV surface antigen for entry — which is why HBV vaccination prevents hepatitis D and why bulevirtide works against it.

Orthopoxvirus monkeypox.entry: Either plasma-membrane fusion or low-pH endosomal entry, using an 11-protein entry-fusion complex.
Orthopoxvirus monkeypox.note: Poxviruses deliberately avoid dependence on one receptor, binding ubiquitous matrix components instead, which is part of why their host and cell range is so broad.

antivirals: Foscarnet and cidofovir for resistant disease
prophylaxis: Suppressive daily antiviral therapy for frequent recurrence
Simplexvirus humanalpha1.note: Antivirals suppress replication and shorten episodes but cannot touch latent genomes in sensory ganglia, so they do not cure or prevent future reactivation. No licensed vaccine, despite repeated attempts.

prophylaxis: Varicella-zoster immunoglobulin for exposed susceptible pregnant women, neonates and the immunocompromised
Varicellovirus humanalpha3.note: The same virus needs two different vaccines: a live one to prevent primary infection in children, and a strongly adjuvanted subunit one to boost waning cellular immunity in older adults and stop reactivation.

prophylaxis: Letermovir prophylaxis after allogeneic stem-cell transplant
CMV immunoglobulin in selected transplant settings
Cytomegalovirus humanbeta5.note: A congenital CMV vaccine is a long-standing priority and none exists; the pentameric complex is the leading immunogen. Letermovir changed transplant practice by being prophylactic without the myelotoxicity of ganciclovir.

Alphapapillomavirus 9.note: Prophylactic only: the L1 virus-like particles prevent establishment but do nothing about existing infection. Single-dose schedules are now WHO-recommended, and countries with early high coverage are already seeing cervical cancer incidence fall.

Rotavirus alphagastroenteritidis.note: Oral vaccines take less well in low-income settings — probably a mixture of maternal antibody, enteric microbiota and HBGA/secretor status — which is the reverse of the pattern for injected vaccines. Intussusception risk is small and outweighed by the benefit.

antivirals: Ribavirin, for chronic hepatitis E in the immunosuppressed (off-label)
Paslahepevirus balayani.note: The only licensed HEV vaccine is available in one country. For travellers there is no vaccine option, so prevention is food and water hygiene — and in pregnancy, where genotype 1 mortality reaches 20-25%, that matters a great deal.

vaccines: Live attenuated RA 27/3, given as MMR
Rubivirus rubellae.note: Vaccination is about preventing congenital rubella syndrome, not the mild childhood illness. The vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy, so the strategy is to immunise before childbearing age.

vaccines: Vimkunya (PXVX0317), virus-like particle, from 12 years of age
IXCHIQ (VLA1553), live attenuated single dose — US licence suspended and the application withdrawn
Alphavirus chikungunya.note: The first chikungunya vaccines, from 2023-2025, and the live one has since been taken off the US market. FDA suspended IXCHIQ's biologics licence on 22 August 2025 after 21 hospitalisations and 3 deaths among reported serious adverse events, one of them an encephalitis death attributed directly to the vaccine with vaccine-strain virus in the cerebrospinal fluid; Valneva withdrew the US licence application and IND on 19 January 2026. Vimkunya, a non-replicating virus-like particle vaccine, is the FDA-approved option. There is still no antiviral, and chronic arthralgia has no specific treatment.

Alphavirus venezuelan.note: No licensed human vaccine; TC-83 and C-84 are investigational and used for laboratory workers under IND.

Alphavirus eastern.note: No licensed human vaccine or antiviral, with case fatality around 30% and severe sequelae in most survivors.

vaccines: 17D live attenuated yellow fever vaccine — single dose, lifelong protection
Orthoflavivirus flavi.note: One of the most effective vaccines ever made, from a 1937 attenuation. Rare but serious adverse events — vaccine-associated viscerotropic and neurotropic disease — concentrate in first-time recipients over 60, which shapes travel-clinic practice.

Orthoflavivirus japonicum.note: No antiviral exists and a third of survivors have permanent neurological sequelae, so prevention is the whole of management.

Orthoflavivirus nilense.note: No human vaccine despite effective equine vaccines, and no antiviral. The commercial case for a human West Nile vaccine has never closed.

vaccines: Qdenga / TAK-003 — approved in the EU, UK and endemic countries
Orthoflavivirus denguei.note: The serostatus restriction on Dengvaxia is the clearest example of antibody-dependent enhancement driving policy: in seronegative recipients the vaccine behaved like a first infection and made a later natural infection worse. No antiviral is licensed; management is fluid balance, and NSAIDs are avoided.

Orthoflavivirus kyasanurense.note: Effectiveness is limited and coverage poor; tick avoidance does most of the work.

Orthoflavivirus zilberi.note: Highly effective but needs a three-dose primary course plus boosters; no post-exposure option exists, so it has to be given before the season.

Orthoflavivirus zikaense.note: No vaccine and no antiviral. Prevention is bite avoidance, and pregnancy-specific travel advice is the main public-health tool.

Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense.note: As for Sudan virus — the Zaire-specific countermeasures do not apply, which is what makes the current DRC outbreak harder than 2018-20.

Orthoebolavirus sudanense.note: No licensed vaccine or therapeutic: ERVEBO and both monoclonals are Zaire-specific. Candidate vaccines were trialled during the 2022 Uganda outbreak.

prophylaxis: Ring vaccination of contacts and contacts of contacts
Orthoebolavirus zairense.note: Both licensed monoclonals and ERVEBO are specific to *Zaire* ebolavirus and do not protect against Sudan, Bundibugyo or Marburg virus — which is why a Bundibugyo outbreak is a far harder problem than a Zaire one. The PALM trial that established them was run during an active outbreak.

Orthomarburgvirus marburgense.note: Nothing licensed. The Sabin and IAVI vaccine candidates were deployed under trial protocols during the Rwanda and Equatorial Guinea outbreaks; remdesivir and MBP091 have animal data only.

Henipavirus nipahense.note: No licensed vaccine or antiviral. m102.4, a human monoclonal, is available on compassionate grounds, and HeV-sG vaccine candidates and remdesivir have animal data. A WHO priority pathogen precisely because of this gap.

vaccines: Live attenuated measles vaccine, given as MMR or MR (Edmonston-Zagreb, Schwarz, Moraten strains)
prophylaxis: Measles immunoglobulin within 6 days of exposure for infants, pregnant women and the immunocompromised
Morbillivirus hominis.note: Two doses give ~97% protection and immunity is lifelong. Vitamin A reduces mortality in children and is a WHO recommendation, but it is not an antiviral. Herd immunity needs about 95% coverage, which is why measles is the first disease to return when coverage slips.

vaccines: Live attenuated mumps vaccine (Jeryl Lynn, RIT 4385, Urabe strains), given as MMR
Orthorubulavirus parotitidis.note: Effectiveness is the weakest component of MMR, around 88% after two doses, and wanes — which is why outbreaks occur in highly vaccinated university populations and why a third dose is used in outbreak control.

Metapneumovirus hominis.note: No licensed vaccine or antiviral, despite a burden comparable to RSV in young children and older adults.

vaccines: Abrysvo (RSVpreF) for older adults and in pregnancy
prophylaxis: Nirsevimab — single-dose long-acting monoclonal for infants
Orthopneumovirus hominis.note: RSV went from having nothing to having several options in two years, once prefusion F was stabilised as an immunogen. Maternal immunisation and infant nirsevimab are alternative routes to the same protection, and the 1960s formalin-inactivated vaccine disaster — enhanced disease on natural infection — is why the field moved so carefully.

prophylaxis: Post-exposure prophylaxis: immediate wound washing, vaccine series, plus human or equine rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound for category III exposures
Lyssavirus rabies.note: Post-exposure prophylaxis is essentially 100% effective if started before symptoms, and once encephalitis begins the disease is effectively always fatal — the widest gap between prevention and treatment in medicine. The Milwaukee protocol is not a treatment.

Orthohantavirus sinnombreense.note: No licensed vaccine or antiviral anywhere; Hantavax, an inactivated HFRS vaccine, is licensed in South Korea and does not cover the Americas. Management is early ECMO for cardiopulmonary syndrome.

vaccines: Hantavax, inactivated — licensed in South Korea only
Orthohantavirus hantanense.note: Hantavax is licensed in South Korea; the efficacy evidence is limited and it is not used elsewhere. No antiviral, and it does not cover the American hantaviruses.

Orthobunyavirus catqueense.note: No vaccine or antiviral, and no reason to expect one for a virus with a single published human case.

Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense.note: No vaccine or antiviral. With the 2024 expansion and reports of vertical transmission this is now a recognised gap.

Mammarenavirus choriomeningitidis.note: No vaccine or licensed antiviral; ribavirin has been used off-label. Prevention is rodent control and screening of transplant donors.

antivirals: Ribavirin — widely used, but the evidence base has been seriously questioned
Mammarenavirus lassaense.note: The ribavirin evidence rests largely on a 1986 study whose analysis has since been challenged; current trials are reassessing it. Several vaccine candidates are in trials, none licensed.

vaccines: Candid#1 live attenuated — licensed in Argentina
antivirals: Immune plasma from convalescent donors, which cuts mortality from ~15-30% to ~1% if given early
Mammarenavirus juninense.note: A rare success: a regionally licensed vaccine plus convalescent plasma turned Argentine haemorrhagic fever from a major rural killer into a controlled disease.

vaccines: Inactivated mouse-brain vaccine (Bulgaria) — not internationally licensed
antivirals: Ribavirin — benefit contested, observational data only
Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae.note: No internationally licensed vaccine or proven antiviral, high case fatality and documented nosocomial spread: the combination is why CCHF is BSL-4 and on the WHO priority pathogen list.

Bandavirus dabieense.note: No licensed vaccine or antiviral. Favipiravir has been trialled in China with uncertain benefit.

Phlebovirus riftense.note: No human vaccine is licensed; veterinary vaccines exist and reduce human exposure by controlling livestock epizootics — a One Health intervention rather than a human one.

vaccines: Inactivated quadrivalent and trivalent, egg- and cell-based
High-dose and adjuvanted formulations for older adults
prophylaxis: Oseltamivir or baloxavir for post-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk contacts
Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae.note: Reformulated annually because of antigenic drift, which is a consequence of the error-prone polymerase and segmented genome. Adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) are no longer used: essentially all circulating A viruses carry the M2 S31N resistance change.

prophylaxis: Pemivibart — monoclonal pre-exposure prophylaxis for the immunocompromised
Betacoronavirus pandemicum.note: Most therapeutic monoclonals, including casirivimab/imdevimab, sotrovimab and bebtelovimab, were withdrawn as spike evolved away from their epitopes. The small-molecule antivirals target conserved enzymes and have held up — a general lesson about where to aim.

Norovirus norwalkense.note: No licensed vaccine or antiviral; candidates are in trials. Management is rehydration, and control is hand hygiene and environmental disinfection — alcohol gel is relatively ineffective against a non-enveloped virus.

vaccines: Oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV, Sabin) — bivalent and monovalent type 2
Novel OPV2 (nOPV2), genetically stabilised against reversion
antivirals: Pocapavir (V-073, SCH-48973) — capsid inhibitor, investigational, used for chronic excretors under compassionate access
V-7404 — protease inhibitor, in development as a combination partner to suppress resistance
Enterovirus coxsackiepol.note: OPV gives mucosal immunity and interrupts transmission, but reverts to cause circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus; IPV protects the individual without stopping gut replication. nOPV2 exists to keep OPV's transmission-blocking without the reversion, and is the main tool against cVDPV2 outbreaks.

Enterovirus deconjuncti.note: No vaccine or antiviral for EV-D68, which is the main concern given its association with acute flaccid myelitis.

prophylaxis: Vaccine or immunoglobulin within 2 weeks of exposure
Hepatovirus ahepa.note: Post-exposure vaccination works because the incubation period is long — roughly 28 days — which gives the immune response time to get ahead of the infection.

prophylaxis: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus vaccine at birth for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers
Orthohepadnavirus hominoidei.note: Suppressive, not curative: nucleos(t)ide analogues control replication but do not clear the integrated or episomal cccDNA reservoir, so treatment is usually lifelong. Birth-dose vaccination is the single most effective intervention against hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide.

Lentivirus humimdef1.note: No vaccine after forty years of trying — the diversity of env and the integrated reservoir defeat it. But treatment is so effective that an undetectable viral load means no sexual transmission, and twice-yearly lenacapavir has shown near-complete protection as PrEP.

vaccines: Prevented entirely by hepatitis B vaccination
Deltavirus italiense.note: The only virus here whose vaccine is another virus' vaccine: HDV cannot infect without HBsAg, so HBV immunisation prevents it absolutely. Bulevirtide blocks the shared NTCP receptor.

antivirals: Tecovirimat — efficacy not demonstrated in the PALM007 and STOMP trials
prophylaxis: Post-exposure MVA-BN within 4 days (ideally), up to 14 days
Orthopoxvirus monkeypox.note: A cautionary case: tecovirimat was widely deployed on the strength of animal data, and the randomised trials in DRC and the US did not show a benefit in clade I or clade II disease. Vaccination remains the effective intervention.

prophylaxis: Vaccinia immune globulin for vaccine complications
Orthopoxvirus variola.note: Eradicated in 1980; the countermeasures exist for biodefence and are what made the 2022 mpox response possible so quickly.

guidelines.title: STI Treatment Guidelines: Genital Herpes

agents.class: Nucleoside analogues activated by viral thymidine kinase
agents.use: Episodic treatment, daily suppression, and intravenous therapy for encephalitis and neonatal disease.
agents.evidence: Intravenous aciclovir reduced mortality in HSV encephalitis from around 70% to 19-28% — one of the largest treatment effects in infectious disease. Suppressive valaciclovir also reduces transmission to a susceptible partner by about 48%.

refs.label: Whitley et al. N Engl J Med 1986 (HSV encephalitis)
Corey et al. N Engl J Med 2004 (transmission)

agents.grade_note: Adequately powered randomised trial evidence with a clinical endpoint, accepted into major guidelines.

agents.use: Aciclovir-resistant disease, usually in immunocompromised patients.
agents.evidence: Case series only; nephrotoxicity is substantial.
agents.grade_note: Non-randomised human data; confounding not excluded.

investigational.note: Active against aciclovir-resistant HSV; phase 3 PRIOH-1 in immunocompromised patients. A distinct target, so no cross-resistance with nucleoside analogues.

refs.label: Wald et al. JAMA 2016 (pritelivir phase 2)

Simplexvirus humanalpha1.note: Antivirals suppress replication but cannot clear latent genomes from sensory ganglia, so they shorten and prevent episodes without curing or stopping future reactivation. Treatment of encephalitis is a time-critical emergency: start on suspicion, before confirmation.

guidelines.title: International Consensus Guidelines on CMV in Solid-Organ Transplantation

agents.use: Treatment and prophylaxis of CMV disease in transplant and advanced HIV.
agents.evidence: Long-established; myelosuppression is the limiting toxicity. Valganciclovir is non-inferior to intravenous ganciclovir for CMV disease in solid-organ transplant.

refs.label: Asberg et al. VICTOR. Am J Transplant 2007

agents.grade_note: Adequately powered randomised trial evidence with a clinical endpoint, accepted into major guidelines.

agents.use: Prophylaxis after allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplant.
agents.evidence: Phase 3: clinically significant CMV infection in 37.5% versus 60.6% with placebo by week 24, with lower all-cause mortality and no myelosuppression — which is what changed transplant practice.

refs.label: Marty et al. N Engl J Med 2017

agents.grade_note: Adequately powered randomised trial evidence with a clinical endpoint, accepted into major guidelines.

agents.use: Refractory or resistant post-transplant CMV.
agents.evidence: SOLSTICE: superior to investigator-assigned therapy for viraemia clearance (55.7% vs 23.9%) with less nephrotoxicity and neutropenia.

refs.label: Avery et al. SOLSTICE. Clin Infect Dis 2022

agents.grade_note: Adequately powered randomised trial evidence with a clinical endpoint, accepted into major guidelines.

Cytomegalovirus humanbeta5.note: Congenital CMV is the commonest infectious cause of childhood sensorineural deafness; valganciclovir for symptomatic congenital disease improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes, and there is still no vaccine.

guidelines.title: Preparedness and Response for Chikungunya Virus Introduction

agents.use: Analgesia; NSAIDs once dengue is excluded. Chronic arthritis is managed rheumatologically.
agents.evidence: No antiviral has shown benefit. Chloroquine was no better than placebo for acute disease or chronic arthralgia; methotrexate has limited evidence in post-chikungunya arthritis.

refs.label: Post-chikungunya chronic arthralgia: frequency and associations. 2026

agents.grade_note: Non-randomised human data; confounding not excluded.

investigational.note: A virus-like particle vaccine is licensed, and the live-attenuated one that came first has been withdrawn from the US market — the therapeutic gap remains complete either way.

Alphavirus chikungunya.note: Months to years of disabling polyarthralgia with no specific treatment is the real burden of this infection, and it is under-recognised relative to the acute illness.

guidelines.title: Dengue: guidelines for diagnosis, treatment, prevention and control

agents.use: Management is careful fluid balance guided by warning signs and haematocrit.
agents.evidence: Judicious crystalloid resuscitation during the critical plasma-leak phase is what reduces mortality. Corticosteroids do not help, and NSAIDs and intramuscular injections are avoided because of bleeding risk.

refs.label: Wills et al. N Engl J Med 2005 (fluid resuscitation)

agents.grade_note: Adequately powered randomised trial evidence with a clinical endpoint, accepted into major guidelines.

investigational.note: Prevented infection in a human challenge model — the first clinical signal for a dengue antiviral.

Orthoflavivirus denguei.note: No antiviral exists for the most common arboviral infection of humans. Everything that reduces dengue mortality is supportive, and it works: case fatality falls below 1% with good fluid management.

guidelines.title: Guidelines for the care and treatment of persons diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C
HCV Guidance: Recommendations for Testing, Managing, and Treating Hepatitis C

agents.use: 8-12 weeks oral therapy, curative across genotypes.
agents.evidence: Sustained virological response above 95% in ASTRAL-1 and ENDURANCE, including in cirrhosis. SVR is a cure: late relapse is rare and fibrosis regresses.

refs.label: Feld et al. ASTRAL-1. N Engl J Med 2015
Zeuzem et al. ENDURANCE-1. N Engl J Med 2018

agents.grade_note: Adequately powered randomised trial evidence with a clinical endpoint, accepted into major guidelines.

Orthohepacivirus hominis.note: The clearest therapeutic success in virology: a uniformly chronic, cirrhosis-causing infection became curable in 8-12 oral weeks within a decade. There is still no vaccine, so elimination depends entirely on finding and treating people.

guidelines.title: Therapeutics for Ebola virus disease: WHO guideline

agents.use: Confirmed Zaire ebolavirus disease, including neonates and pregnancy.

Alphavirus.name: Alphavirus antigenic complexes
Alphavirus.extent: Strong within complexes, weak between them
Alphavirus.basis: E1 and E2 glycoprotein epitopes. The Semliki Forest complex (chikungunya, o'nyong-nyong, Ross River, Mayaro, Semliki Forest, Getah) cross-reacts internally; the Western equine encephalitis and Venezuelan equine encephalitis complexes each do the same.
Alphavirus.effect: Chikungunya and o'nyong-nyong serology are hard to separate in Africa, where both circulate, and Mayaro is readily mistaken for chikungunya in South America — the clinical pictures are also similar, so serology is doing real diagnostic work and cannot be trusted alone.
Alphavirus.resolution: Neutralisation against a panel; virus-specific RT-PCR in the short viraemic window.

Orthoflavivirus.name: Flavivirus (genus-wide)
Orthoflavivirus.basis: Shared epitopes on envelope protein E, especially the highly conserved fusion loop in domain II.
Orthoflavivirus.effect: IgM and IgG ELISA and immunofluorescence cross-react heavily across the whole genus. A secondary flavivirus infection, or infection in someone vaccinated against yellow fever or Japanese encephalitis, can produce broadly positive serology with no reliable indication of which virus is responsible. Dengue-Zika confusion during the 2015-16 epidemic was the clearest example, and it mattered because the pregnancy implications differ completely.
Orthoflavivirus.resolution: Plaque-reduction neutralisation (PRNT) against a panel, with a four-fold-or-greater titre difference; RT-PCR on an acute specimen, which is specific but has a short window; NS1 antigen for dengue specifically.
Orthoflavivirus.aside: Fusion-loop cross-reactivity is also functional, not just diagnostic: cross-reactive non-neutralising antibody is the proposed mechanism for antibody-dependent enhancement between dengue serotypes, and the reason Dengvaxia is restricted to the seropositive.

Lyssavirus.name: Lyssavirus phylogroups
Lyssavirus.extent: Partial, and split along phylogroup lines
Lyssavirus.basis: Glycoprotein G antigenic sites. Phylogroup I (rabies, Duvenhage, European bat lyssaviruses 1 and 2, Australian bat lyssavirus, Irkut) is cross-neutralised by rabies vaccine-induced antibody. Phylogroup II (Mokola, Lagos bat) and the divergent West Caucasian bat virus and Ikoma lyssavirus are not.
Lyssavirus.effect: This is a prophylaxis question before it is a diagnostic one. Standard rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin protect against phylogroup I exposures, and cannot be relied on for Mokola, Lagos bat virus or West Caucasian bat virus. Serology using rabies antigen may also miss infection by divergent members.
Lyssavirus.resolution: Virus-specific RT-PCR and sequencing; lyssavirus-specific neutralisation assays.
Lyssavirus.aside: It also means the containment calculus differs: a Mokola exposure in a vaccinated worker is not reassuring, which is why atlas.biosafety flags the vaccine as unreliable there.

Orthohantavirus.name: Hantavirus serogroups
Orthohantavirus.basis: Nucleocapsid protein is broadly cross-reactive; the Gn/Gc glycoproteins are more type-specific.
Orthohantavirus.effect: N-based IgM/IgG assays detect hantavirus infection well but often cannot say which species, so the clinical syndrome and the geography carry much of the identification — haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia versus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas.

California serogroup.name: California serogroup
California serogroup.effect: La Crosse, Jamestown Canyon and snowshoe hare virus serology cross-react, so paediatric encephalitis attributed to La Crosse on ELISA alone may be another member.

Simbu serogroup.name: Simbu serogroup
Simbu serogroup.basis: Shared nucleocapsid (N) and Gc glycoprotein epitopes; the serogroup was defined by exactly this cross-reaction before sequencing existed.
Simbu serogroup.effect: IgG ELISA and complement fixation cannot separate members. Reported human seroprevalence for any one Simbu virus may reflect exposure to another — directly relevant to Oya and Cat Que virus, where the human evidence is largely serological, and to Oropouche, which circulates in the same regions as other Simbu viruses.
Simbu serogroup.resolution: Virus neutralisation against a panel of serogroup members, or species-specific RT-PCR on the S segment.
Simbu serogroup.aside: Reassortment compounds the problem: Simbu viruses exchange whole segments, so a virus can carry the N antigen of one parent and the glycoproteins of another — Iquitos and Ngari viruses arose this way.

Mammarenavirus.name: Arenavirus Old and New World groups
Mammarenavirus.extent: Broad on NP, narrow on GP
Mammarenavirus.basis: Nucleoprotein is cross-reactive across the genus; glycoprotein responses are largely species-specific.
Mammarenavirus.effect: Immunofluorescence using one arenavirus antigen may detect infection by another, which matters where Lassa and non-pathogenic Mopeia or Mobala virus co-circulate in the same Mastomys populations.
Mammarenavirus.resolution: Species-specific RT-PCR; neutralisation, which is technically difficult for arenaviruses.

Phlebovirus.name: Phlebovirus sandfly fever complexes
Phlebovirus.extent: Within the Naples and Sicilian complexes
Phlebovirus.basis: Shared N and glycoprotein epitopes. Toscana virus sits within the sandfly fever Naples complex.
Phlebovirus.effect: Toscana virus serology cross-reacts with sandfly fever Naples virus, so Mediterranean seroprevalence studies conflate them; Sicilian virus is antigenically separate.
Phlebovirus.resolution: Neutralisation; virus-specific RT-PCR on CSF for Toscana meningitis.

Alphacoronavirus.name: Human coronaviruses
Alphacoronavirus.extent: Moderate within genus, mostly on nucleocapsid
Alphacoronavirus.basis: N protein is conserved within each genus; the spike receptor-binding domain is not.
Alphacoronavirus.effect: Pre-pandemic sera contain antibody cross-reactive with SARS-CoV-2 N, which confounded early seroprevalence work. Seasonal betacoronavirus exposure also primes cross-reactive T cells.
Alphacoronavirus.resolution: Spike-RBD-specific assays; neutralisation against the relevant variant.

Orthopoxvirus.name: Orthopoxvirus (genus-wide)
Orthopoxvirus.basis: Extensive shared antigens across the orthopoxviruses.
Orthopoxvirus.effect: Serology cannot distinguish mpox from vaccinia vaccination or cowpox, which made serosurveys during the 2022 mpox outbreak nearly uninterpretable in anyone previously vaccinated.
Orthopoxvirus.resolution: Species-specific real-time PCR, which is the diagnostic standard; sequencing for clade assignment.
Orthopoxvirus.aside: The same cross-reactivity is why smallpox vaccination protects against mpox — the diagnostic nuisance and the prophylactic benefit are the same phenomenon.
